stories.title: Yellow rain, wind warning in effect for Leinster, Munster
stories.summary: A Status Yellow rain and wind warning is in effect for Leinster and Munster as Storm Austen tracks over Ireland. Orange warnings for Cork, Dublin, Kerry, Waterford, Wicklow and Wexford expired earlier this morning, with no significant wind or flooding damage being reported. Met Éireann forecast "intense rain" associated with Storm Austen and had warned of the risk of flooding due to fallen leaves and blocked drains. ESB Networks said that as of 7am, around 3,000 homes, farms and businesses were without electricity as a result of Storm Austen. It said there may be further power outages as weather warnings remain in place. ESB Networks crews are on the ground to carry out work to restore power.

stories.title: Foul play ruled out over deaths of man, woman in Bray
stories.summary: Gardaí have ruled out foul play in their investigation into the deaths of a couple in their home in Bray yesterday morning. Bridgid 'Biddy' O'Brien and her partner James McGinn were found dead at their home in the Cois Cairn estate at around 8am on Tuesday. The couple lost their two children in a fire in Dublin nine years ago. Gardaí are satisfied that nobody else was involved in their deaths and are working to establish all the circumstances surrounding their deaths. However, the case is being treated as a tragedy and the Garda Family Liaison Officer is working with the families. The post-mortem examinations have been conducted but preliminary results are not being released for operational reasons.

stories.title: No measure can ease pain of scoliosis failures - minister
stories.summary: The Minister for Health has acknowledged that no measures the Government may introduce will alleviate the pain endured by those affected by failures in spina bifida and scoliosis services. She told the Dáil that stakeholders will be consulted by her officials, who will work with the Attorney General to draft terms of reference for a commission of inquiry. The minister was speaking during Statements on Children's Health Ireland (CHI), which was also attended in the visitors' gallery by some of those who have been advocating for action on the matter. Ms Carroll MacNeill said that she received the final scoping report on 9 September, and expressed her gratitude to Remy Farrell SC for his efforts to "capture the pain" and "very real frustration" of those affected. She noted that a commission of investigation, as recommended by Mr Farrell, allows for greater flexibility than a tribunal, including private hearings. She noted that witnesses can request whether to have their testimony heard in public or private.

stories.title: Japan inflation accelerates, paving way for rate hike
stories.summary: Inflation in Japan accelerated sharply in September, official data showed today, rising above the Bank of Japan's target level and paving the way for a further interest rate hike. The acceleration was driven in particular by rising prices for processed foods against a backdrop of soaring energy costs due to conflict in the Middle East. Excluding volatile fresh produce, inflation was 2.1%, up from 1.7% in August, according to the internal affairs ministry reading. The figure was in line with market expectations and above the 2% target set by the central bank, further raising chances of an interest rate hike. "With underlying inflation back above the Bank of Japan's 2% target, the case for further tightening remains on solid ground," said Abhijit Surya of Capital Economics. "News reports suggest that the Bank may revise up its inflation forecasts at its October meeting. That should set the stage for another hike in December," he added.

stories.title: France reports first death of human from Shamonda virus
stories.summary: French health authorities said that the Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, had been detected in a human for the first time, in a severely immunocompromised patient who died earlier this month. There was "no health risk to the general public identified at this time", the health and agriculture ministries said in a joint statement. It added that the human infection appeared to be "an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient" hospitalised for a serious medical condition. "Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans," the ministries said. The virus, which belongs to the Orthobunyavirus group and is typically transmitted to animals by small biting insects, was first detected in Europe this summer, they said. At this stage in the investigation, the patient was believed to have contracted the virus through the bite of a midge in eastern France, where the virus was circulating in animals during the spring and summer, the ministries said.

stories.title: Rovers may win the league but challengers are improving
stories.summary: Whatever happens over the final two games, I think this League of Ireland season deserves a closer look than simply asking whether Shamrock Rovers have won another title. They remain the benchmark. Their consistency over several seasons has earned them that status. But beneath them, something is changing. Clubs are becoming better equipped to compete, talent is spreading around the division, and the numbers suggest that challenging Rovers is becoming a more realistic ambition. If you're a maths head - you may enjoy some of the figures below that back the above sentence up. With two games remaining, they have 62 points. That already exceeds every total they recorded across the previous five seasons. Last year they finished with 54. In 2024 it was 42. Even their strongest return during that period, 58 in 2023, has been surpassed. They have also scored 60 goals, 12 more than last season, with two matches still to play. Whatever disappointment might accompany finishing second, that is substantial progress.

stories.summary: Aston Villa boss Unai Emery believes the confidence of his players is improving after they continued their impressive start to the Champions League campaign with a 3-1 victory over Viking. They picked up their latest win thanks to Ross Barkley’s opener and Emi Buendia’s penalty, as well as an own goal from Henrik Heggheim. Villa would have finished the night top of the Champions League table but for Viking’s Peter Christiansen replying late which also denied them a third straight clean sheet. Emery admits there is still work to do but his side took another step forward. He said: "We are delighted how we are responding to our demands. stories.title: Ireland call-ups for uncapped pair McNabney and Benson
stories.summary: Uncapped Ulster pair James McNabney and Jamie Benson have both been included in Ireland's squad for next month's Nations Championship games, with Jack Conan ruled out due to injury. Conan, who picked up a shoulder injury in Leinster's 48-23 win away to Clermont Auvergne last weekend, will miss the four-game November window, with Harry Byrne, Jack Crowley, Caelan Doris, and Bryn Ward among those who also miss out due to injury. Utility back Benson, who joined Ulster from Harlequins this summer, has made four appearances for Richie Murphy's side this season between centre and out-half, and the versatile former England Under-20 international can also cover full-back. McNabney (23), who has previously been involved with Ireland squads as a training panellist, is named in the squad by Farrell after impressing on his return from an ACL injury, which saw him miss out on the entire 2025/26 campaign. "It's always great to give people a chance for the first time," head coach Andy Farrell said. "Jamie Benson came into camp with us in the summer before we went away, so it was great to get to know him and see what he's all about. But he started the season really well in a few different positions for Ulster, so that shows his versatility.

stories.title: Michael Fry on sketch comedy and Christmas panto ambitions
stories.summary: Matthew Dinneen, known to the world as Michael Fry, has been growing his profile in Ireland since the online comedy boom of 2020. During the pandemic, his satirical internet sketches and musical parodies made him viral, with sketches ranging from the absurd (his Halloween stint as a Joe Duffy-style presenter on a supernatural radio show) to incredibly catchy recreations of pop culture moments (he wrote an Indie banger based on a moment from the British reality show Come Dine With Me). TV opportunities arrived soon after, with his first small screen role landing in 2021 on Callan Kicks the Years, followed by appearances on Derry Girls, Good Boy, and Darren & Joe's Free Gaff. In the years that followed, Fry took to the stage of Vicar Street, taking the crown in Tony Cantwell's mock Eurovision competition, Bureau De Change; he brought his Indie boy band to Whelan's to perform his parody hit, and he appeared on The Late Late Show to sing his Irish take on Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire. Outside of music, the Meath man has taken steps to further his career in both live comedy and entertainment. In 2025, he enjoyed his first solo outing on stage, bringing his hour, Fry Me to The Moon, to the Edinburgh Fringe Festival - the world's largest performing arts festival - before signing up for a stint on Dancing with the Stars Ireland in 2026.

stories.summary: Announcing this week's line-up, the Late Late said: "Mayo actor Philippa Dunne will make her Late Late debut on Friday night. She has become one of Ireland's best-loved comedy stars with knockout performances in Derry Girls, Tall Tales & Murder, and Amandaland. She'll tell us about her BAFTA nod and working with her comedy heroes. "Also joining Patrick on Friday night are Ireland's Premier couple Mikey Breen and Sharlene Mawdsley. Both sports stars have represented county and country - Mikey has lifted the Liam McCarthy Cup for Tipperary three times while athlete Sharlene has wowed in the athletics world in recent years. They'll chat about competing on the national and international stage and why they'll always be each other's biggest supporters. The pair will also be put through their paces in a unique sporting challenge. "Host of Ireland's Fittest Family Laura Fox will drop by ahead of the 14th season of the hit TV series returning next month. She'll dish all the backstage gossip and explain why some of the coaches are more difficult to keep in check than others. She'll also talk of her joy at getting married earlier this year. "Traditional Irish music group Beoga will be in studio for a music performance and a chat. The band made headlines around the world recently when they took a stand for what they believe in and walked away from Ed Sheeran's tour, amid controversy over the singer's removal of Macklemore from his touring line-up. "As he prepares to take part in the Dublin Marathon, Iain Ward, known to millions of his followers as The King of Chemo, will discuss the life-changing diagnosis that sent him on a path that has taken him around the world raising money for cancer research. "With the devastating consequences of drug-related intimidation in Ireland making weekly headlines, Investigations Editor of The Sunday World Nicola Tallant will be in studio to talk about the rise in violent crime and the communities across the country that are living in fear.

stories.title: Mescal to produce film starring 13 intellectually disabled actors
stories.summary: Mary is Missing follows an ensemble immersed in a crime thriller with delicious twists and turns. Now, with Paul Mescal involved, could Oscar success be imminent? Kate Demolder writes. Could it be that, at long last, we’re finally starting to see people with disabilities given opportunities to shine on screen? If a successful cultural transformation can be defined as the moment when actors of all kinds are in front of the camera, in roles not centred on their perceived differences, then Mary is Missing might just be one of those hallowed pieces that is ushering in a new era. Mary is Missing is an Oscar-qualified Irish short film that features an ensemble of Irish intellectually disabled performers, including award-winning Irish actor and theatre maker Mark Smith – known for his semi-autobiographical one-man stage show Making a Mark – as well as Derek McSweeney, Eoghan Ashe, Ella-Jane Moore, Jackie O’Hagan, John Egan, Keith Foley, Maurice Coll, Neil Coffey, Teresa Flood, Wesley Fairbrother, Lucy Smith and Conor Begley. "We’re down to the wire now," Smith says of the impending wait for the Academy Award shortlist, announced on December 16. "But... It’s very exciting." The film centres on Yellow Tree Day Service care worker Mary, who hasn’t turned up for work two days in a row. When Garda Foley is called, he and the care team begin investigating the conflicting accounts of the service’s users – to uncover not just what happened, but why they might be hiding the truth. The plot hails from a writers’ room with the film’s cast at Run of the Mill, the award-winning and inclusive theatre company based out of The Mill Community Centre in Celbridge and Maynooth University.

stories.title: Rise in young people being seriously injured on roads
stories.summary: The Road Safety Authority has said there has been an increase in serious injuries among young drivers aged 17 to 25 since 2020. Almost a third suffer serious injuries if they are involved in a crash, more than any other age group. The RSA analysis shows that 28% suffered clinically serious injuries, a higher share than for any other age group of drivers. Serious head injuries and chest injuries were most common, requiring lengthy hospital stays with potential for life-long consequences. The RSA also expressed concerns among older pedestrians, with figures showing that over a third of the 29 pedestrians who were killed so far this year, were over the age of 65. Seán O'Leary is a 27-year-old former Kerry footballer whose life was upended after he was involved in car crash in 2021.

stories.title: Ex-PTSB CEO wins appeal over Central Bank inquiry finding
stories.summary: Former Permanent TSB chief executive David Guinane has won an appeal against the findings of a Central Bank inquiry over his role in PTSB's treatment of tracker mortgage customers during the financial crisis. Last year a Central Bank inquiry found that Mr Guinane participated in regulatory breaches by the lender relating to its treatment of tracker mortgage customers between 2009 and 2010. He was the first individual to face an inquiry for their role in the tracker mortgage controversy and to be found to have participated in any breaches. Mr Guinane was subsequently fined €80,000 and was subject to a reprimand. However, the former PTSB CEO appealed the decision of the inquiry to the Irish Financial Services Appeals Tribunal (IFSAT), which has now overturned it. In a decision published on its website, the Tribunal concluded that the Central Bank inquiry "erred in law; acted ultra vires and unreasonably" and "failed to give fair notice of certain issues; and failed to give reasons" for its decision.

stories.title: Stack 'badly failed' by investigation into his murder
stories.summary: Prison officer Brian Stack was "badly failed" by the investigation into his murder in the 1980s, the Taoiseach has said as he delivered a State apology to his family. Mr Stack, the chief prison officer in Portlaoise, was shot in the neck by the IRA in March 1983 and died 18 months later. Micheál Martin delivered a State apology to the Stack family and said: "It is plainly and utterly unacceptable that material that was potentially of evidential value to the investigation can no longer be located by An Garda Síochána. "It is admitted by An Garda Síochána that these are serious matters that had an impact on the investigation. "As Taoiseach, and on behalf of the Government I want to formally apologise to the Stack family for these failings." The Stack family described the State apology as a "deeply emotional day for the family".

stories.title: Apple launches into foldable market with iPhone Duo
stories.summary: Sales of Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, begin today, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones. The Duo's reception could prove an early test for new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September. It could also have large implications for a niche category in which ⁠rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for several years. Within minutes of pre-orders opening last Friday, Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response from customers "nothing short of extraordinary." In Sydney, the first Apple store to sell the phones today, a queue of customers formed outside before opening at 8am local time. In China, a soft consumer market combined with memory costs pushing prices higher has led to six quarters of declines in a row in smartphone shipments.

stories.title: Meta ordered to pay $25bn in user data privacy case
stories.summary: A judge in the US state of New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion (€22.2bn) after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The ruling comes two months after Meta agreed to pay $18bn to settle claims brought by 48 other states, including allegations tied to Cambridge Analytica. "This ruling... makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Meta said in a statement. "We are confident we will prevail on appeal." Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting firm found to have improperly harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users for targeted political advertising, notably during the 2016 US presidential election. Revelations at the time showed that the firm had obtained data gathered through a personality quiz app called "thisisyourdigitallife", which was installed by about 270,000 users but also collected information on their friends. In total, the app reached roughly 87 million Facebook users worldwide.

stories.title: LOI previews: Rovers close in and relegation six-pointer
stories.summary: St Patrick's Athletic defeat at the Brandywell on Monday evening has left us with more or less a two-horse race as we hit the final week of the Airtricity League Premier Division season. Champions Shamrock Rovers occupy the driver's seat, three points clear of Bohemians and six clear of third-placed Pat's with just two games apiece to play. Down at the other end, third-bottom Waterford host second-bottom Drogheda with the pair locked together on points and fighting desperately to avoid the relegation playoff. Stephen Bradley seemed content enough last week when declaring that, should his side take care of business in the their remaining games, they "know what that brings". They're one-third of the way through their final hat-trick of fixtures, which began with a surprise 2-0 loss in Galway. However, a Hoops win at home to Sligo this evening and the Tallaght men will have a firm hand on their sixth title in seven seasons.

stories.title: Majority of county players against further rule changes
stories.summary: The majority of male inter-county Gaelic footballers are opposed to any further rule changes, with those in support only favouring small tweaks, according to the GPA's Member Survey Report 2026. Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group have proposed 11 changes to the rules which are currently being trialled in the third level Division 1 league. The rule tweaks, aimed at curbing slow attacks, include a rule limiting the number of consecutive handpasses to three, a ban on fisted points and the reintroduction of the four-point goal. However, 76% of male players surveyed by the GPA are opposed to further rule changes, with 23.5% suggesting that small tweaks are needed. Just 0.5% players surveyed feel that significant changes are needed. In hurling, there is majority support for just three potential changes, with two-thirds of those surveyed favouring the return of the maor foirne, while 58% support a change to allow seven substitutions rather than five. A very slight majority (51%) favour the introduction of two-point sideline cut.

stories.title: United defeated again as Como pile pressure on Carrick
stories.summary: Manchester United fell to one of the most embarrassing European defeats in their history as Champions League upstarts Como ran out 4-1 victors to heap pressure on head coach Michael Carrick. The under-fire Red Devils boss had felt Sunday's purposeful point at rivals Leeds marked a "fresh start" after Lisandro Martinez highlighted the club’s shortcomings in a set of stunning interviews last week. But United instead saw their wretched start to the season hit a new low on Wednesday as Cesc Fabregas’ Como punished a display devoid of shape, grit and skill to extend their winless run to a seventh match. This humbling loss puts Carrick’s future under intense scrutiny, with the storm that battered the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia nothing compared to the one brewing at Old Trafford. United made a nightmare start, just as they did at Atletico Madrid last week, as burgeoning star Nico Paz struck against a side that were shaky out of possession and shapeless with it. Carrick’s side were fortunate to only be a goal behind at the break and their luck soon ran out, with Tasos Douvikas’ strike followed by Paz scoring his second and Jacobo Ramon heading home.

stories.title: Connacht's Jansen backed to fill number 8 gap for Ireland
stories.summary: Andy Farrell's back row depth will be put to the test next month, with Jack Conan joining Caelan Doris on the sidelines for the Nations Championship slate of games in November. Leinster and the IRFU are yet to put a timeline on Conan's recovery from the shoulder injury he picked up in the province's impressive win against Clermont Auvergne last weekend, but the 34-year-old will miss the four-game slate next month, left out of the 36-man squad. Quite a few of the back row forwards selected by Farrell have experience packing down at the base of the scrum, with Cian Prendergast, Nick Timoney and the uncapped James McNabney all wearing 8 for their provinces on occasion, although Connacht's Sean Jansen appears to be leading the race to start the opening game of the block against Argentina on Friday, 6 November. The 27-year-old starred on his debut for Ireland against Japan in Australia in July, with his try-scoring man of the match display earning him a place on the bench against the All Blacks a week later. The New Zealand native, who qualified for Ireland through his grandparents from Belfast and Monasterevin, scored 12 tries in 20 games for Connacht last season, and was a key player for Stuart Lancaster's side as they secured Champions Cup qualification. The powerful back row has continued to be effective for the province in the early stages of this season, starting each of their last three games since returning to duty, helping them to wins against Benetton and Saracens.

stories.title: How a historic Killarney hotel transformed into a 5-star spot
stories.summary: Charlotte Ryan visits the Great Southern Hotel in Killarney Co Kerry, a luxury destination steeped in history and visited by celebrity guests, months after it achieved its 5-star rating to learn about the process. The last time I had been in the Great Southern in Killarney, it was for a very different affair: a two-day wedding in 2022 that saw us dance until 3am, play music together until 4am, come in from the thumping noise of JM Reidy's on the main street and throw ourselves, smelling of late night chips and cigarette smoke, on plush couches in the lobby, before attempting the slog back to our rooms. This time, however, I was greeted at the train station - a literal stone's throw away from the hotel's front door - by a concierge, who carried my bags to reception, where I was handed a welcome cocktail and serenely talked through the plan for that evening: a champagne toast, a three-course gala dinner and a night cap in the hotel's cosy bar. The difference in experiences, of course, says everything about me and nothing about the Great Southern, a sumptuous Killarney institution that has long prided itself on being a 4-star hotel with a 5-star spirit. Now, however, that 5-star rating is firmly part of its story and I had been invited to stay at the hotel and attend its celebratory dinner that night. The rating was awarded in June 2026, a milestone moment two-years in the making. It was clearly a huge moment for the staff, some of whom have been with the Great Southern for over 57 years, says General Manager Jamie Power, with at least 20 of the 200-strong staff there for "well over 30 years".

stories.title: Trump ordered to testify in BBC defamation case
stories.summary: A US judge has issued President Donald Trump a deadline to testify under oath in his $10 billion (€8.91bn) defamation lawsuit against the BBC. Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Mr Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including cancelling a previously agreed date of 16 October. If he fails to attend the deposition by 11 December, he risks sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said. The US President has accused the BBC of deceptively editing its documentary 'Trump: A Second Chance' to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on 6 January 2021, after losing the presidential election. The crowd proceeded to storm the US Congress in an attempt to disrupt the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden's victory. stories.title: Sakila died from number of factors, inquest hears
stories.summary: A man who became unresponsive while being detained by security staff in Dublin city centre earlier this year died from a number of factors, including a cardio-respiratory arrest, after being restrained in a prone position, an inquest has heard. The opening of the inquest into the death of Yves Sakila at Dublin District Coroner's Court also heard that his body has still not been buried due to the failure of his family to reach agreement on the issue. The fatal incident occurred on Henry Street, Dublin 1 shortly after 5pm on 15 May. Gardaí were alerted to the scene after the 34-year-old had been detained by security staff over an alleged shoplifting incident in Arnotts. Another man, aged in his 80s, was injured as Mr Sakila was attempting to flee the scene. Mr Sakila subsequently became unresponsive at the scene and was brought by ambulance to the Mater Hospital where he was pronounced dead a short time later.

stories.title: Legislation to remove Triple Lock passes Dáil vote
stories.summary: Legislation to scrap the Triple Lock has passed its first vote in the Dáil after 79 TDs backed the change and 71 opposed it. The Triple Lock only allows the deployment of more than 12 members of the Defence Forces overseas when it has been agreed by the Government, the Dáil and the UN. The Bill, which will end the requirement for UN approval, will be further scrutinised at the Committee Stage most likely next month. It is expected the contentious legislation will be enacted before the end of the year. The Opposition was united in objections to the Bill saying it was an erosion of the country's military neutrality. The Government insisted the change was necessary in order to allow Ireland to continue sending peacekeepers overseas.

stories.title: Volvo Cars to cut 2,500 jobs amid third quarter loss
stories.summary: Volvo Cars said today it will cut 2,500 jobs, mostly in its native Sweden, as the group seeks to slash costs amid tough competition from Chinese auto makers and as tariffs and weak demand hit sales in the US. The company, majority-owned by China's Geely Holding, reported an adjusted operating loss of 3.7 billion Swedish crowns ($373 million) for the third quarter, down from a profit of 5.8 billion crowns a year earlier. Volvo said that in addition to its earlier cost reductions it will cut an additional 5 billion crowns in indirect spend and variable costs, which it expects to be realised by the end of next year. Some 2,500 jobs will be lost globally, of which 2,000 are in Sweden as the group ends consultant contracts, applies natural attrition and offers "targeted exit packages" to employees, Volvo Cars said in a statement. The group has long struggled to stay profitable amid cooling demand for electric vehicles (EV), tough conditions in China - where revenue fell by almost 50% in the third quarter - and the strain of high costs and tariffs. "The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs a decisive reinforcement," CEO Hakan Samuelsson said.

stories.title: Russian strikes show 'no change' in Kremlin position
stories.summary: Ukraine has accused Russia of failing to change its position on the war, by firing a wave of ballistic missiles just after US envoy Steve Witkoff met President Vladimir Putin to discuss the resumption of peace talks. Air raid sirens sounded throughout the night and into the day in Kyiv, where two people were killed and more than 30 other people wounded, city authorities said. Two women aged 50 and 60 were killed and dozens more people were wounded in an attack on a crowded market in the eastern city of Lozova. Two were wounded in the Moscow region after Ukraine launched its own large-scale drone attack. The strikes came after the Kremlin said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month, but dismissed new ideas brought by Mr Witkoff that were developed with European countries and Ukraine. In all, a dozen Ukrainian regions were hit overnight, including residential houses, energy sites, shops, cafes and a monastery damaged in Kyiv, where strikes have intensified before winter sets in. All families and children were told to evacuate the frontline towns of Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk in the east after a spate of attacks killed dozens of civilians.

stories.title: Harnedy: Hard to step away when Cork are so close
stories.summary: Cork stalwart Seamus Harnedy said it was extra-hard to step away from the county set-up because "the lads are so close" to the ultimate glory. However, the three-time All-Star made the call to retire from the inter-county game after what he described as a "tough" year in which his game-time was severely limited. The 36-year old had been battling injuries in recent seasons but was deployed as a sub in the 2025 All-Ireland final. However he wasn't introduced at any stage in this summer's All-Ireland semi-final loss to Galway, as Cork floundered in the second half. Harnedy acknowledges that in the immediate aftermath of the Galway game, this would likely be his last involvement with the Cork set-up as a player. "After the Galway game, I probably knew that was it," Harnedy told reporters ahead of the Ireland-Scotland hurling/shinty clash this weekend.

The 36-year old had been battling [[gortuithe|injuries]] in recent seasons but was deployed as a sub in the 2025 All-Ireland [[cluiche ceannais|final]]. However he wasn't introduced at any stage in this summer's All-Ireland semi-final loss to Galway, as Cork floundered in the second half.
